newsitem.title: USA: FCOJ futures end down sharply in technical trade.
newsitem.headline: FCOJ futures end down sharply in technical trade.

text.p: FCOJ July futures settled sharply lower in a technically-driven selloff led by the speculators, floor sources said.

The benchmark July contract closed 1.65 cents lower at 77.80 cents per lb, having ranged from 79.90 to 77.40 cents. September finished down 1.55 cents at 80.10 cents, while the remaining months settled 1.35 and 1.45 weaker.
Volume was estimated at a brisk 7,500 lots compared with Thursday's official 2,382 lots.

Light local buying carried the July contract to a high of 79.90 cents, a 38 percent retracement of the 10.5 cent move lower. But speculative selling eroded the underlying support and pressured the market to the day's low.
Analysts expect the market to fall to support betweem 75.00 and 74.00 cents in July.
Technically, July has slipped below its 40-day and 50-day moving averages, while an increasingly negative global supply and demand situation weighs on the market, analysts said.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture will release its next crop estimate on June 12, with no change expected from the previous report. The USDA put Florida's crop at a record 224.2 million 90-lb boxes and yields at 1.58 gallons per box.
Output in Brazil was pegged at 1.2 million tonnes in 1997/98, compared with 1.1 million tonnes this year.
"This is the first time that both of the world's largest producers of oranges will have back-to-back bumber harvests," Merrill Lynch Judith Ganes, noted in a weekly citrus report.
Meanwhile, retail prices are too high to boost weak demand of orange juice in the U.S.

Market analysts dismissed the effect of the Medfly, spotted in Florida citrus this week, on prices. They said the pests could only have a negative effect on prices, since they damage fresh fruit which would then be sent to be processed.

Ganes added that "history has shown that support from these features should be very short-lived, and while there is always the fear of plagues destroying the crop, actual damage tends to be non-existant and simply costs the state of Florida millions of dollars to eradicate the problem."
